title: Generate & Filter Relevant Ideas
outcome: Independently produce at least three plausible ideas, judge task relevance, improve a vague idea when appropriate, choose one idea and explain fit; rejection is never compulsory.

teaching.microLesson1: Brainstorming has two different actions: make possibilities, then examine them. Do not reject everything just to fill a box.
teaching.microLesson2: Choose one idea using the actual task, audience and resource constraints; explain why it fits. All candidates may be valid and set-aside can remain blank.

demo.prompt: A small community centre wants a free activity for families on a rainy Sunday afternoon. Suggest one activity and explain why it fits.

steps.label: Notice
steps.text: It must work indoors, be free or inexpensive, and suit families. The Task is to suggest one activity, not to describe a personal memory.

steps.label: Generate without grading
steps.text: Board-game circle; family storytelling hour; simple recycled-paper crafts; community football match.

steps.label: Filter
steps.text: First three can work indoors. The football match conflicts with a rainy indoor setting unless it is redesigned for a gym, and may be impractical for a small centre.

steps.label: Repair
steps.text: Community football match could become indoor mini-ball skills with soft equipment, but that raises space/safety questions. Repair is possible; not compulsory.

steps.label: Choose
steps.text: Recycled-paper crafts is easy to start using available paper, takes place indoors and works for different ages. No invented participant numbers or cost claims.

steps.label: Transfer thinking
steps.text: A different prompt may make the football idea suitable. Relevance depends on the actual task, not a global good/bad label.

teaching.commonMistake: Write the first interesting idea regardless of audience, limits or explainability.
teaching.a1: Ideas can begin as keywords. Optional starter: This idea fits because ...
teaching.b1: Compare two valid ideas under one realistic constraint (space, safety, time, cost) and justify a trade-off.

cycleA.prompt: Your school wants one affordable improvement to its outdoor break-time area. Suggest a change that makes that outdoor area more useful for students.
cycleA.instructions: Sort the six cards into FITS, NEEDS_DETAIL_OR_REPAIR or OFF_TASK. Read feedback for every card, then repair A2 or A6 in your own words and explain one classification. Alternative defensible interpretations may be explained in the open note.

cards.text: Put simple benches beside the playground trees so students have somewhere to sit.
cards.rationale: Specific outdoor improvement serving break-time use; price still needs checking in real planning
Still about the right setting, but does not say what change to make

cards.text: Change the timetable for school buses.
cards.rationale: A transport change, not an improvement to the outdoor area

cards.text: Paint simple hopscotch grids on an empty part of the playground.
Build a new cinema inside the library.
cards.rationale: Interior entertainment facility, not the outdoor break area

cards.text: Add some equipment to the playground.
cards.rationale: Could fit, but type, location and practical benefit are unspecified

cycleA.repairPrompt: Choose A2 or A6. Write a more specific improvement in your own words; many valid repairs exist.
cycleA.justificationPrompt: I placed card ___ in ___ because the task says ___.

cycleB.prompt: Your local library wants one new weekend activity that helps teenagers enjoy reading. Suggest an activity and explain why it would suit the library.
cycleB.instruction: Enter at least three different candidate activities as short notes; decide whether each Fits, Needs clarification or is Off-task. Choose one and explain why it suits the library and teenagers. Set aside an idea only if useful; this is entirely optional. Make one vague idea more concrete in your own words.
cycleB.choiceRationalePrompt: This activity matches the library and teenagers because ...
cycleB.setAsidePrompt: Optional: Which idea would you set aside, even if relevant, and what trade-off explains your decision? Leave blank if all ideas fit.
cycleB.concretePrompt: Develop one vague idea into a more concrete action, in your own words.
cycleB.allValid: Book-swap table, short graphic-novel circle and read-and-draw session may all fit. Never force a reject or prefill these in student fields.
cycleB.completion: Three distinct nonempty notes, a chosen index that exists, and a nonempty fit rationale; process-only, not a quality or CEFR verdict.

transfer.prompt: A neighbourhood youth group wants a low-cost outdoor activity for a Saturday morning. Suggest one activity and explain why young people could join easily.
transfer.instruction: Save three NEW candidates, choose one, and give a fresh selection rationale. Do not copy library activities; no forced reject.

supplemental.title: Relevance to a specific task
supplemental.prompt: Suggest one improvement to a small public reading room.
supplemental.question: Which is clearly on task?

options.text: Add a shelf for shared books
Change the city football team's uniform

supplemental.title: Repair a vague idea
supplemental.prompt: Suggest an activity for a rainy lunch break in a classroom.
supplemental.question: Which revision makes 'something fun' most usable for this task?

options.text: It is fun and very good.
options.rationale: Repeats evaluation without identifying any activity
Still lacks the action and classroom fit

options.text: Play a short classroom word-guessing game using the board.
options.rationale: Names an indoor activity and usable materials

options.text: Students should buy a different school uniform.

supplemental.title: Choose and explain a trade-off
supplemental.prompt: A small library with limited tables wants a weekend activity. Two ideas are a book-swap table and a very large dance performance.
supplemental.question: Which explanation best justifies choosing the book-swap?

options.text: Book swaps are the best because they are best.
It can use the few tables the library already has, while the dance performance needs more space.

options.rationale: Personal dislike does not explain feasibility

options.text: My cousin once visited a library.

supplemental.title: All-valid ideas and optional rejection
supplemental.prompt: Select a quiet weekend library activity. Learner proposes a book discussion, bookmark-making and picture-book storytelling.
supplemental.question: Which action shows appropriate idea selection?

options.text: Label one of the three ideas off-topic even if it fits, because a reject box must be filled
options.rationale: Fabricates a bad idea when all three can suit the library

options.text: Refuse to choose until an impossible idea is invented
options.rationale: Brainstorming does not require a deliberately bad idea

options.text: Choose one and explain why it suits the audience and resources; leave rejection blank if useful
Copy every idea into a final essay without selecting
options.rationale: The task asks for one chosen activity

aiCriteria.review: Do candidates address the exact library/activity task? Is choice explained by audience/resources? Does vague repair become concrete?
aiCriteria.avoid: Never require Off-task or setAside, never use number of ideas to claim quality, never invent feasibility data or ghostwrite an idea.
aiCriteria.question: You wrote 'reading games.' What would teenagers do during this activity?
aiCriteria.acceptAllValid: If three ideas fit and setAside is empty, explicitly accept this as valid process outcome.
aiCriteria.fallback: AI review is currently unavailable. Your draft is saved locally; you can continue editing or finish the lesson.
